nameStory: Grey seals get their name from their mottled grey coat, which can range from silvery-grey to dark charcoal. They're also known as "horsehead seals" because of their distinctively long, horse-like snouts. The scientific name Halichoerus grypus translates to "hook-nosed sea pig," which isn't exactly flattering but captures their distinctive curved nose profile!
description: Grey seals are large, robust marine mammals that belong to the "true seals" or "earless seals" family. These impressive animals have torpedo-shaped bodies built for life in the ocean, with powerful flippers for swimming and no external ears. Adult males can reach up to 8 feet long and weigh over 600 pounds, while females are typically smaller at around 6 feet and 400 pounds. Their most striking feature is their distinctively long, Roman-nosed snout that gives them an almost horse-like profile when viewed from the side.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Large, barrel-shaped body with a distinctively long snout that looks almost horse-like in profile. Males are significantly bulkier than females, with thick necks and broader heads.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Mottled grey coat that can range from light silvery-grey to dark charcoal, often with darker spots or patches. When dry, the fur feels coarse and thick to help insulate against cold water.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen hauled out in groups on rocky shores, beaches, or floating docks, basking in the sun. They're surprisingly agile on land despite their bulk, using their front flippers to pull themselves along.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found along rocky coastlines, sandy beaches, and increasingly on man-made structures like docks and breakwaters. Look for them in areas where they can easily slip into deep water.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Leave distinctive drag marks in sand or mud from their bodies and flippers. Their hauling-out spots often smell strongly of fish and have a musky, marine odor that carries on the wind.

habitat: Grey seals prefer rocky coastlines, sandy beaches, and increasingly use human-made structures like floating docks, breakwaters, and piers throughout New England's coast. They need areas where they can easily access deep water for fishing but also have suitable spots to haul out and rest. You'll most commonly spot them from Maine down to Cape Cod, especially around islands and protected coves.

seasonality.spring: Peak pupping season occurs from January through March, so spring is when you might see mothers with their white-coated pups on secluded beaches. Adults are actively feeding and rebuilding energy after the breeding season.
seasonality.summer: Most active time for feeding and hauling out to bask in warm weather. Large groups gather on favorite beaches and rocky outcrops, making this the best time for wildlife watching.
seasonality.fall: Adults are building up fat reserves for winter breeding season. You may notice increased activity and more aggressive behavior as breeding season approaches.
seasonality.winter: Breeding and pupping season when seals spend more time on land. Males establish territories and can be quite vocal and aggressive during this time.

funFact: Grey seals can hold their breath for up to 40 minutes and dive as deep as 500 feet to hunt for fish, using their sensitive whiskers to detect the water movements made by swimming prey even in complete darkness!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with harbor seals, but grey seals are much larger with distinctively long, horse-like snouts compared to harbor seals' shorter, dog-like faces. Remember: "Grey seals have long noses like horses, harbor seals have short noses like dogs."
contextualKnowledge: In the United States, this species is spelled "gray seal," while in other English-speaking countries it's "grey seal." They're also sometimes called Atlantic seals or horsehead seals, but all refer to the same species that was once heavily hunted and has made a remarkable recovery in New England waters.
compareHints: Grey seals are the only species in their genus, making them unique among seals. Compared to their closest relatives in the earless seal family, like harbor seals, grey seals are significantly larger and have that distinctive elongated snout. Unlike eared seals (sea lions), grey seals have no external ears and move on land by sliding on their bellies rather than "walking" on their flippers.
